## 2. Rank 2 scattering diagrams and theta functions

In this section, we review rank-2 scattering diagrams, broken lines and theta functions. Generalized cluster scattering diagrams in rank 2 are studied in detail in Section 2.2, whose cluster complex structure leads to the definition of rank-2 generalized cluster algebras in Section 2.3.

### 2.1. Scattering diagrams in rank 2

We introduce basic notions of rank-2 scattering diagrams following [24, Section 6.3]. Fix a rank- $2$ lattice $M\cong\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ and let $N=\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb{Z})$ . Let $\mathscr{P}$ be a finitely generated monoid equipped with a map

$$ r\colon\mathscr{P}\rightarrow M. $$

Denote by $\mathscr{P}^{\times}$ the group of units in $\mathscr{P}$ . Let $\mathfrak{m}$ denote both the monoid ideal $\mathscr{P}\cut\mathscr{P}^{\times}$ in $\mathscr{P}$ and the monomial ideal $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}\cut\mathscr{P}^{\times}]$ in the monoid algebra $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]$ over a ground field $\Bbbk$ of characteristic zero. Let

$$ \widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}\coloneqq\lim_{\longleftarrow}\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k} $$

be the $\mathfrak{m}$ -adic completion of $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]$ .

We say a monomial ideal $I$ in $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]$ is $\mathfrak{m}$ -primary if its radical $\sqrt{I}$ is $\mathfrak{m}$ .

#### Definition 2.1.

Fix $r\colon\mathscr{P}\rightarrow M$ and let $I$ be an $\mathfrak{m}$ -primary ideal. A ray or line, uniformly referred to as a wall, over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I$ or $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ is the data $\mathfrak{d}$ of

- • the support $S_{\mathfrak{d}}\subseteq M_{\mathbb{R}}\coloneqq M\otimes\mathbb{R}$ given by

$$ S_{\mathfrak{d}}=b-\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}m_{\mathfrak{d}}\quad\text{or}\quad S_{\mathfrak{d}}=b-\mathbb{R}m_{\mathfrak{d}} $$

for some $b\in M_{\mathbb{R}}$ and the direction $-m_{\mathfrak{d}}\in M\cut\{0\}$ ;

- • the wall-function $f_{\mathfrak{d}}$ is an element in $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I$ or in $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ such that

$$ f_{\mathfrak{d}}=1+\sum_{m\in\mathscr{P}({m_{\mathfrak{d}}})}c_{m}x^{m} $$

where $\mathscr{P}({m_{\mathfrak{d}}})\coloneqq\{m\in\mathscr{P}\mid r(m)\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}m_{\mathfrak{d}}\}$ and $f_{\mathfrak{d}}\equiv 1\mod\mathfrak{m}$ .

#### Remark 2.2.

A ray does not start at the origin when $b\neq 0$ and a line does not cross the origin when $b\notin\mathbb{R}m_{\mathfrak{d}}$ . A wall $\mathfrak{d}$ is sometimes represented by the pair $(S_{\mathfrak{d}},f_{\mathfrak{d}})$ , but two walls can have the same pair of support and wall-function.

#### Definition 2.3.

A scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}$ over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I$ is a finite set of walls over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I$ . A scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}$ over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ is a countable set of walls over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ such that for each $k\geq 0$ , the subset

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{k}\coloneqq\{\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}\mid f_{\mathfrak{d}}\not\equiv 1\mod\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}\} $$

is a scattering diagram over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ .

#### Definition 2.4.

The support of $\mathfrak{D}$ is defined as

$$ \operatorname{Supp}(\mathfrak{D})\coloneqq\bigcup_{\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}}S_{\mathfrak{d}}\subseteq M_{\mathbb{R}}. $$

The singular locus $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D})$ of $\mathfrak{D}$ is the union of the boundary point of every ray and the zero-dimensional intersection locus of any pair of walls.

Associated to a wall $\mathfrak{d}$ over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I$ or $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ and a vector $v\in M_{\mathbb{R}}$ transversal to $S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ is the wall-crossing automorphism $\mathfrak{p}_{v,\mathfrak{d}}\in\operatorname{Aut}(\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I)$ or $\operatorname{Aut}(\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]})$ . It is an algebra automorphism defined by

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{v,\mathfrak{d}}(x^{m})\coloneqq x^{m}f_{\mathfrak{d}}^{n\cdot r(m)}\quad\text{for}\quad m\in\mathscr{P}, $$

where $n\in\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb{Z})$ is primitive and orthogonal to $S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ such that $n\cdot v<0$ , where $\cdot$ denotes the natural pairing between $\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb{Z})$ and $M$ . Clearly $\mathfrak{p}_{v,\mathfrak{d}}^{-1}=\mathfrak{p}_{-v,\mathfrak{d}}$ .

A path (a smooth immersion) $\gamma\colon[0,1]\rightarrow M_{\mathbb{R}}$ is called regular with respect to a scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}$ over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I$ if it is a smooth immersion such that

- • $\gamma([0,1])\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D})=\varnothing$ and $\{\gamma(0),\gamma(1)\}\cap\operatorname{Supp}(\mathfrak{D})=\varnothing$ ;

- • it crosses walls only transversally.

For a regular path $\gamma$ , let

$$ 0<t_{1}\leq\cdots\leq t_{s}<1 $$

be a sequence of maximal length such that $\gamma(t_{i})\in S_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}$ for some wall $\mathfrak{d}_{i}\in\mathfrak{D}$ and that if $t_{i}=t_{j}$ , then $\mathfrak{d}_{i}$ and $\mathfrak{d}_{j}$ are two distinguished elements in $\mathfrak{D}$ .

The path-ordered product of $\gamma$ is defined to be

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}\coloneqq\mathfrak{p}_{\dot{\gamma}(t_{s}),\mathfrak{d}_{s}}\circ\cdots\circ\mathfrak{p}_{\dot{\gamma}(t_{1}),\mathfrak{d}_{1}}\in\operatorname{Aut}(\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I)\,, $$

where $\dot{\gamma}(t)$ denotes the tangent vector $\frac{d\gamma(t)}{dt}$ . The order of $\mathfrak{p}_{\dot{\gamma}(t_{i}),\mathfrak{d}_{i}}$ and $\mathfrak{p}_{\dot{\gamma}(t_{j}),\mathfrak{d}_{j}}$ in the product when $t_{i}=t_{j}$ is irrelevant because they commute in $\operatorname{Aut}(\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I)$ .

A path $\gamma$ is regular with respect to a scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}$ over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ if it is regular with respect to $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ for each $k\geq 0$ . The path-ordered product of $\gamma$ is defined to be

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}\coloneqq\lim_{\longleftarrow}\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}_{k}}\in\operatorname{Aut}(\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]})\,, $$

where each $\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}_{k}}$ is considered to be in $\operatorname{Aut}(\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1})$ .

#### Definition 2.6.

Two scattering diagrams $\mathfrak{D}$ and $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ (both over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I$ or $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ ) are said to be equivalent and denoted as $\mathfrak{D}\equiv\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ if

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}=\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}} $$

for any path $\gamma$ that is regular to both.

In view of the above equivalence, it is convenient to consider a “wall” with support $S_{\mathfrak{d}}=b+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}m_{\mathfrak{d}}$ and wall-function $f_{\mathfrak{d}}$ . It does not qualify either as a line or a ray in Definition 2.1, but is equivalent to the union of a line and a ray

$$ \{(b+\mathbb{R}m_{\mathfrak{d}},f_{\mathfrak{d}})\}\cup\{(b+\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m_{\mathfrak{d}},f_{\mathfrak{d}}^{-1}). $$

#### Definition 2.8.

A scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}$ is called consistent if the path-ordered product $\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}$ is the identity for any regular path $\gamma$ that is a closed loop, or, equivalently, $\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}$ only depends on the endpoints $\gamma(0)$ and $\gamma(1)$ .

#### Remark 2.9.

It is straightforward to see that $\mathfrak{D}$ is consistent if and only if each $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ is consistent. By definition, $\mathfrak{D}_{0}$ is empty. If $\mathfrak{D}_{1}$ only consists of lines, then it is consistent because wall-crossing automorphisms in $\operatorname{Aut}(\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{2})$ commute.

The following theorem is due to Kontsevich and Soibelman [31]. The version adopted below can be found in [24, Theorem 6.38] where an order-by-order algorithmic construction is given; see also [29, Theorem 1.4].

#### Theorem 2.10.

Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be a scattering diagram (over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I$ or $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ ). There always exists a consistent scattering diagram $\Scat(\mathfrak{D})$ unique up to equivalence such that $\Scat(\mathfrak{D})\cut\mathfrak{D}$ consists only of rays.

The above theorem implies that $\Scat(\mathfrak{D})$ only depends on the lines in $\mathfrak{D}$ because for any ray in $\mathfrak{D}$ one can always add another ray with the exact same support but with the inverse wall-function to cancel out their contribution to any path-ordered product.

Theorem 2.10 is functorial in the following sense.

In the complete case, suppose that we have $\varphi\colon\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}_{1}]}\rightarrow\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}_{2}]}$ such that $\varphi(\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}_{1}(m)]})\subseteq\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}_{2}(m)]}$ for any $m\in M\cut\{0\}$ . For $\mathfrak{D}$ a scattering diagram over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}_{1}]}$ , we have

$$ \Scat(\varphi(\mathfrak{D}))\equiv\varphi(\Scat(\mathfrak{D})), $$

as scattering diagrams over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}_{2}]}$ by Theorem 2.10, where the operation $\varphi$ keeps the support of a wall and applies the map $\varphi$ to the attached wall-function.

### 2.2. Generalized cluster scattering diagrams

In this subsection, we study a particular class of scattering diagrams that are relevant to generalized cluster algebras in rank 2. They are fundamental to our study of positivity in more general cases.

Let $M=\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ with the standard unit vectors $e_{1}=(1,0)$ and $e_{2}=(0,1)$ . Let $\ell_{1}$ , $\ell_{2}$ be positive integers. Choose the monoid

$$ \mathscr{P}=\mathscr{P}_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}=M\oplus\mathbb{M}_{1}\oplus\mathbb{M}_{2} $$

with $r\colon\mathscr{P}\rightarrow M$ the projection to $M$ , where $\mathbb{M}_{i}$ is the (multiplicative) monoid of monomials in variables $\{p_{i,k}\mid 0\leq k\leq\ell_{i}\}$ . We set conventionally $p_{i,0}=1$ , thus $\mathbb{M}_{i}\cong\mathbb{N}^{\ell_{i}}$ . The monoid $\mathbb{M}_{i}$ embeds in $\mathbb{P}_{i}\cong\mathbb{Z}^{\ell_{i}}$ the group of Laurent monomials. Denote

$$ \mathbb{M}=\mathbb{M}_{1}\oplus\mathbb{M}_{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{P}_{1}\oplus\mathbb{P}_{2}. $$

To express monomials in $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]$ , let $x$ and $y$ denote respectively the monomials associated to $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ in $M$ .

#### Definition 2.12.

The generalized cluster scattering diagram associated to the pair $(\ell_{1},\ell_{2})$ is the consistent scattering diagram $\Scat(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})$ over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ (up to equivalence) where

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}\coloneqq\{(\mathbb{R}e_{1},P_{1}),(\mathbb{R}e_{2},P_{2})\}, $$

$$ P_{1}=1+\sum_{k=1}^{\ell_{1}}p_{1,k}x^{k}\quad\text{and}\quad P_{2}=1+\sum_{k=1}^{\ell_{2}}p_{2,k}y^{k}. $$

This scattering diagram (and its close variants) has been considered many times in different contexts, for example in [29, 28, 49, 40, 11]. Since it is determined by the initial wall-functions $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ , we denote it by $\Scat(P_{1},P_{2})$ . This notation will be further extended to $\Scat(f_{i}\mid i\in I)$ for a collection of wall-functions $\{f_{i}\mid i\in I\}$ , which represent the lines (through the origin) they determine. This specializes to the ordinary cluster scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{(\ell_{1},\ell_{2})}$ (cf. [27]) when $P_{1}=1+x^{\ell_{1}}$ and $P_{2}=1+y^{\ell_{2}}$ .

#### Remark 2.14.

Note that we are using the $d$ -vector version of the scattering diagram rather than the $g$ -vector version, see [10] for a comparison.

Following the Kontsevich–Soibelman algorithm explained in the proof of [24, Theorem 6.38], one can choose $\mathfrak{D}=\Scat(P_{1},P_{2})$ (in its equivalent class) so that any added ray in $\mathfrak{D}\cut\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}$ has support in the strict third quadrant and is pointed at the origin, i.e., of the form $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)$ for $(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{2}$ . Further, rays with identical support can be combined into one ray by multiplying their wall-functions together. Therefore, we can assume that $\mathfrak{D}$ has distinct rays with non-trivial wall-functions $f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}$ . It is convenient to assign degrees $\deg p_{1,k}=\deg p_{2,k}=k$ , and thus a multi-degree in $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ to any (Laurent) monomials in $\mathbb{P}$ so that for a monomial term $px^{ka}y^{kb}$ in $f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}$ , the multi-degree of $p$ is $(ka,kb)$ by homogeneity constraints.

A first step towards understanding the structure of $\mathfrak{D}$ is the following mutation operation. Take a representative of $\mathfrak{D}$ as

$$ \{(\mathbb{R}e_{1},P_{1})\}\cup\{(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}e_{2},P_{2})\}\cup\{(\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b),f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)})\mid a\geq 0,b>0\}, $$

where $(a,b)$ is over all primitive vectors such that $f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}$ is non-trivial. Namely we break the wall $(\mathbb{R}e_{2},P_{2})$ into two halves. The positive half is a wall in the sense of (2.7) and the negative half is included in the third subset of the above union.

Define the piecewise linear transformation $T\colon M_{\mathbb{R}}\rightarrow M_{\mathbb{R}}$ by for $(a_{1},a_{2})\in M_{\mathbb{R}}$ ,

$$ T(m)\coloneqq\begin{cases}(a_{1},a_{2})\quad&a_{2}\geq 0,\\
(a_{1}-\ell_{1}a_{2},a_{2})\quad&a_{2}\leq 0.\end{cases} $$

Define the monoid $\mathscr{P}^{\prime}\coloneqq M\oplus{\mathbb{M}}^{\prime}_{1}\oplus\mathbb{M}_{2}$ with the projection $r^{\prime}\colon\mathscr{P}^{\prime}\rightarrow M$ , where ${\mathbb{M}}^{\prime}_{1}$ is the monoid of monomials in $\{p_{1,k}/p_{1,\ell_{1}}\mid 0\leq k\leq\ell_{1}\}$ . Let $P^{\prime}_{1}=P_{1}/(p_{1,\ell_{1}}x^{\ell_{1}})\in\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}^{\prime}]}$ .

Define the collection

$$ T(\mathfrak{D})\coloneqq\{(\mathbb{R}(-e_{1}),P^{\prime}_{1})\}\cup\{(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}e_{2},P_{2})\}\cup\{(\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}T((a,b)),T(f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}))\mid a\geq 0,b>0\}, $$

where $T(f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)})(x,y)=f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}\left(x,y/(p_{1,\ell_{1}}x^{\ell_{1}})\right)$ .

#### Theorem 2.16.

The set $T(\mathfrak{D})$ is a scattering diagram over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}^{\prime}]}$ . Furthermore it is equivalent to $\Scat(P^{\prime}_{1},P_{2})$ as scattering diagrams over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}^{\prime}]}$ .

#### Proof.

In the context of cluster scattering diagrams of Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich, this result is well-known as the mutation invariance [27, Theorem 1.24]. In principle one obtains a similar proof which involves generalizing the very hard Theorem 1.28 in loc. cit. Here we are in rank 2 so a simpler argument is available although more complex initial wall-functions are allowed.

It suffices to show that (1) $T(\mathfrak{D})$ is indeed a scattering diagram over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}^{\prime}]}$ and then (2) it is consistent and contains the same collection of lines as $\Scat(P^{\prime}_{1},P_{2})$ . To show (1), we check that each pair

$$ \left(\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}T((a,b)),T(f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)})\right) $$

qualifies as a wall over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}^{\prime}]}$ . Let $px^{ka}y^{kb}$ be a monomial in a non-trivial $f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}$ . It gets transformed by $T$ into

$$ pp_{1,\ell_{1}}^{-kb}x^{ka-\ell_{1}kb}y^{kb}, $$

which can be induced by the map

$$ T\colon M\oplus\mathbb{P}\rightarrow M\oplus\mathbb{P},\quad(m,p_{1},p_{2})\mapsto(T(m),p_{1}p_{1,\ell_{1}}^{-\deg p_{2}},p_{2}). $$

It is enough to show that the first entry of the multi-degree of $pp_{1,\ell_{1}}^{-kb}$ is always non-positive. This is equivalent to

$$ ka-\ell_{1}kb\leq 0\iff a/b\leq\ell_{1}, $$

which follows directly from [28, Corollary 6]. This also implies that every ray of $T(\mathfrak{D})$ lies in the fourth quadrant. Notice that as in (2.7) the wall $(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}e_{2},P_{2})$ in $T(\mathfrak{D})$ is equivalent to

$$ \{(\mathbb{R}e_{2},P_{2})\}\cup\{(\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}e_{2},P_{2}^{-1})\}. $$

Hence $T(\mathfrak{D})$ and $\Scat(P^{\prime}_{1},P_{2})$ can be regarded to have the same set of lines.

It only remains to show the consistency, that is, $\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,T(\mathfrak{D})}=\operatorname{id}$ for a simple loop $\gamma$ around the origin. This can be checked analogously as in Step II of the proof of [27, Theorem 1.24], which essentially follows from the consistency of $\mathfrak{D}$ . ∎

One immediate consequence of Theorem 2.16 is

$$ f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(\ell_{1},1)}=1+\sum_{k=1}^{\ell_{2}}p_{1,\ell_{1}}^{k}p_{2,k}x^{\ell_{1}k}y^{k}, $$

which follows from $T(f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(\ell_{1},1)})=P_{2}$ .

We also know from the proof of Theorem 2.16 that $\mathfrak{D}$ has no ray in the interior of

$$ \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}}\{(-1,0),(-\ell_{1},-1)\}. $$

Such a region will be called a “chamber” and many more can be obtained by applying iterative mutations of scattering diagrams as follows.

Let ${\mathbb{M}}^{\prime}_{2}$ be the monoid of monomials in $\{p_{2,k}/p_{2,\ell_{2}}\mid 0\leq k\leq\ell_{2}\}$ . Let $P^{\prime}_{2}\coloneqq P_{2}/(p_{2,\ell_{2}}y^{\ell_{2}})$ . Denote for $i\in\mathbb{Z}$ ,

$$ \mathfrak{D}^{(i)}\coloneqq\begin{cases}\Scat(P_{1},P_{2})\\
\Scat(P^{\prime}_{1},P_{2})\\
\Scat(P^{\prime}_{1},P^{\prime}_{2})\\
\Scat(P_{1},P^{\prime}_{2})\end{cases}\ \text{over}\quad\mathscr{P}^{(i)}\coloneqq\begin{cases}M\oplus\mathbb{M}_{1}\oplus\mathbb{M}_{2}\\
M\oplus\mathbb{M}_{1}^{\prime}\oplus\mathbb{M}_{2}\\
M\oplus\mathbb{M}_{1}^{\prime}\oplus\mathbb{M}_{2}^{\prime}\\
M\oplus\mathbb{M}_{1}\oplus\mathbb{M}_{2}^{\prime}\end{cases}\ \text{for}\quad i=\begin{cases}0\mod 4\\
1\mod 4\\
2\mod 4\\
3\mod 4.\end{cases} $$

This periodic sequence of scattering diagrams can be seen as obtained by iteratively applying mutations in Theorem 2.16. We denote by $T_{i}$ the mutation operation turning $\mathfrak{D}^{(i)}$ into $\mathfrak{D}^{(i+1)}$ analogous to the mutation $T$ defined earlier from $\mathfrak{D}^{(0)}$ to $\mathfrak{D}^{(1)}$ . It involves a piecewise linear map $T_{i}\colon M_{\mathbb{R}}\rightarrow M_{\mathbb{R}}$ as in (2.15) and a group homomorphism $T_{i}\colon M\oplus\mathbb{P}\rightarrow M\oplus\mathbb{P}$ as in (2.17). The composition $T_{i+3}T_{i+2}T_{i+1}T_{i}$ does not act on $M_{\mathbb{R}}$ by the identity map. Hence it sends a wall $\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}^{(i)}$ to another one with different support, giving non-trivial implication on the structure of $\mathfrak{D}^{(i)}$ .

We use the above idea to generate a $\mathbb{Z}$ -sequence of “chambers” in $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{D}^{(0)}$ . A connected component in the complement of the closure of a scattering diagram’s support is called a chamber. Each $\mathfrak{D}^{(i)}$ has a positive chamber $\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{C}^{(i)})$ , the interior of the cone $\mathcal{C}^{(i)}$ non-negatively spanned by the incoming halves of the two initial walls, that is, the $(i+1)$ -th (modulo $4$ ) quadrant in $M_{\mathbb{R}}=\mathbb{R}^{2}$ . Define piecewise linear maps on $M_{\mathbb{R}}$ for $i\geq 1$

$$ T^{(i)}\coloneqq T_{i-1}\cdots T_{1}T_{0},\quad T^{(-i)}=T_{-i}^{-1}\cdots T_{-1}^{-1},\quad\text{and}\quad T^{(0)}=\mathrm{id}. $$

Define for $i\in\mathbb{Z}$ cones

$$ \mathcal{C}_{i}\coloneqq\left(T^{(i)}\right)^{-1}\left(\mathcal{C}^{(i)}\right)\subseteq M_{\mathbb{R}}. $$

Namely, we pull back $\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{C}^{(i)})$ via the piecewise linear transform $T^{(i)}$ to obtain a chamber $\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{C}_{i})$ in $\mathfrak{D}$ . Every $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{i+1}$ intersect at their common boundary, which is either the support of a ray or a half line in $\mathfrak{D}$ . The associated wall-function can also be obtained by pulling back from the initial wall-functions in $\mathfrak{D}^{(i)}$ . The cones $\{\mathcal{C}_{i}\mid i\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ form a discrete part of $\mathfrak{D}$ , which is referred to as the cluster complex of $\mathfrak{D}$ where $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ is called a cluster cone while its interior is called a cluster chamber. The map $T^{(4)}\colon M_{\mathbb{R}}\rightarrow M_{\mathbb{R}}$ acts on the cluster complex such that $T^{(4)}(\mathcal{C}_{i+4})=\mathcal{C}_{i}$ .

When $\ell_{1}\ell_{2}<4$ , there are only finitely many $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ and their union is $M_{\mathbb{R}}$ . Thus there are finitely many rays in $\mathfrak{D}\cut\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}$ . We depict in Figure 1 the case $\ell_{1}=3$ and $\ell_{2}=1$ . All the remaining cases can be obtained by specializing certain $p_{i,j}$ to zero (by the functoriality) and possibly switching $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ . In Figure 1, the added rays are

$$ \displaystyle\left(\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(3,1),\ 1+p_{1,3}p_{2,1}x^{3}y\right), \displaystyle\left(\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(2,1),\ 1+p_{1,2}p_{2,1}x^{2}y+p_{1,1}p_{1,3}p_{2,1}^{2}x^{4}y^{2}+p_{1,3}^{2}p_{2,1}^{3}x^{6}y^{3}\right), \displaystyle\left(\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(3,2),\ 1+p_{1,3}p_{2,1}^{2}x^{3}y^{2}\right), \displaystyle\left(\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(1,1),\ 1+p_{1,1}p_{2,1}xy+p_{1,2}p_{2,1}^{2}x^{2}y^{2}+p_{1,3}p_{2,1}^{3}x^{3}y^{3}\right). $$

*Figure 1. $\Scat(P_{1},P_{2})$ , where $P_{1}=1+p_{1,1}x+p_{1,2}x^{2}+p_{1,3}x^{3}$ and $P_{2}=1+p_{2,1}y$ .*

When $\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\geq 4$ , the structure of the cluster complex is summarized in Theorem 2.21, for which we need some preparation. Define vectors ${\mathbf{d}}_{n}=(d_{1;n},d_{2;n})\in M=\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ by setting initially

$$ {\mathbf{d}}_{0}=e_{2},\quad{\mathbf{d}}_{1}=-e_{1},\quad{\mathbf{d}}_{2}=-e_{2},\quad{\mathbf{d}}_{3}=e_{1}, $$

and for $n\neq 1,2$

$$ {\mathbf{d}}_{n+1}+{\mathbf{d}}_{n-1}=\begin{cases}\ell_{1}{\mathbf{d}}_{n}\quad&\text{when $n$ is odd},\\
\ell_{2}{\mathbf{d}}_{n}\quad&\text{when $n$ is even}.\end{cases} $$

The following properties of $d_{n}$ are easily obtained by induction.

#### Lemma 2.19.

We have (1) ${\mathbf{d}}_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{2}$ for $n\neq 0,1,2,3$ ; (2) $\{{\mathbf{d}}_{n},{\mathbf{d}}_{n+1}\}$ is a basis of $M$ ; (3) for $n\neq 0,1,2,3$ ,

$$ \begin{cases}d_{1;n}/\ell_{1},\ (d_{2;n}-1)/\ell_{2}\in\mathbb{N},\quad&n\equiv 0\mod 4,\\
(d_{1;n}+1)/\ell_{1},\ d_{2;n}/\ell_{2}\in\mathbb{N},\quad&n\equiv 1\mod 4,\\
d_{1;n}/\ell_{1},\ (d_{2;n}+1)/\ell_{2}\in\mathbb{N},\quad&n\equiv 2\mod 4,\\
(d_{1;n}-1)/\ell_{1},\ d_{2;n}/\ell_{2}\in\mathbb{N},\quad&n\equiv 3\mod 4.\end{cases} $$

We define

$$ \overline{P}_{1}(z):=\frac{1}{p_{1,\ell_{1}}}z^{\ell_{1}}P_{1}(z^{-1})\quad\text{and}\quad\overline{P}_{2}(z):=\frac{1}{p_{2,\ell_{2}}}z^{\ell_{2}}P_{2}(z^{-1}). $$

Notice that they both have constant term $1$ . For $(u,v)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ , let $W((u,v))=p_{1,\ell_{1}}^{u/\ell_{1}}p_{2,\ell_{2}}^{v/\ell_{2}}$ .

#### Theorem 2.21.

Outside the closed cone “Badlands”

$$ C_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}\coloneqq\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}}\left\{\left(2\ell_{1},\ell_{1}\ell_{2}+\sqrt{\ell_{1}^{2}\ell_{2}^{2}-4\ell_{1}\ell_{2}}\right),\left(\ell_{1}\ell_{2}+\sqrt{\ell_{1}^{2}\ell_{2}^{2}-4\ell_{1}\ell_{2}},2\ell_{2}\right)\right\}, $$

the rays in $\mathfrak{D}\cut\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}$ are precisely

$$ \left\{\left(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}d_{n},\zeta_{n}(x^{d_{1;n}}y^{d_{2;n}})\right)\,\middle|\,n\in\mathbb{Z}\cut\{0,1,2,3\}\right\} $$

where for $n\neq 1,2$ ,

$$ \zeta_{n}(z)\coloneqq\begin{cases}P_{2}(W({\mathbf{d}}_{n}-e_{2})z)\quad&n\equiv 0\mod 4,\\
\overline{P}_{1}(W({\mathbf{d}}_{n}+e_{1})z)\quad&n\equiv 1\mod 4,\\
\overline{P}_{2}(W({\mathbf{d}}_{n}+e_{2})z)\quad&n\equiv 2\mod 4,\\
P_{1}(W({\mathbf{d}}_{n}-e_{1})z)\quad&n\equiv 3\mod 4.\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

When $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are binomials, this structure is well-known from [27, Example 1.15]; see also [10, Section 4]. When $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are monic polynomials, this result can already be extracted from [28, Section 5]. In the current setting, the stated description of rays is obtained by working out the cones $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ , $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ and the wall-functions on their boundary rays. Inductively we have

$$ \mathcal{C}_{n}=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}}\{{\mathbf{d}}_{n+1},{\mathbf{d}}_{n+2}\}. $$

The attached wall-functions on $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}{\mathbf{d}}_{n}$ are also obtained inductively from iterative mutations in Theorem 2.16. Notice that there is no ray in the interior of $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ . The limits of $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}{\mathbf{d}}_{n}$ when $n\rightarrow+\infty$ and $n\rightarrow-\infty$ are respectively the two boundaries of $C_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}$ (which degenerates to a single ray when $\ell_{1}\ell_{2}=4$ ). Therefore we have exhausted all added rays outside $C_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}$ . ∎

The next two examples are when $\ell_{1}\ell_{2}=4$ . In these cases, the cluster complex is infinite but the cone $C_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}$ is one-dimensional.

#### Example 2.22.

Let $\ell_{1}=\ell_{2}=2$ . We take the initial wall-functions

$$ P_{1}=(1+s_{1}x)(1+s_{2}x)\quad\text{and}\quad P_{2}=(1+t_{1}y)(1+t_{2}y), $$

which are related to the polynomials in (2.13) by the substitution

$$ p_{1,1}=s_{1}+s_{2},\quad p_{2,1}=t_{1}+t_{2},\quad p_{1,2}=s_{1}s_{2},\quad p_{2,2}=t_{1}t_{2}. $$

The closed cone $C_{2,2}$ is a single ray $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(1,1)$ . The associated wall-function is computed by Reineke and Weist [49] to be

$$ \displaystyle f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(1,1)} \displaystyle=\frac{(1+s_{1}t_{1}xy)(1+s_{1}t_{2}xy)(1+s_{2}t_{1}xy)(1+s_{2}t_{2}xy)}{(1-s_{1}s_{2}t_{1}t_{2}x^{2}y^{2})^{4}} \displaystyle=\frac{(p_{1,1}p_{2,2}xy^{2}+p_{2,1}y)(p_{1,2}p_{2,1}x^{2}y+p_{1,1}x)}{(1-p_{1,2}p_{2,2}x^{2}y^{2})^{4}}+\frac{1}{(1-p_{1,2}p_{2,2}x^{2}y^{2})^{2}}. $$

We see that in the expansion (where $x$ and $y$ are omitted), every coefficient is a polynomial of $p_{1,1},p_{1,2},p_{2,1},p_{2,2}$ with nonnegative integer coefficients:

$$ \sum_{k\geq 0}(k+1)p_{1,2}^{k}p_{2,2}^{k}+\left[\binom{k+3}{3}+\binom{k+2}{3}\right]p_{1,1}p_{2,1}p_{1,2}^{k}p_{2,2}^{k}\\
+\binom{k+3}{3}p_{2,1}^{2}p_{1,2}^{k+1}p_{2,2}^{k}+\binom{k+3}{3}p_{1,1}^{2}p_{1,2}^{k}p_{2,2}^{k+1}. $$

A combinatorial interpretation of each term is given in Theorem 5.17. The objects corresponding to $(k+1)p_{1,2}^{k}p_{2,2}^{k}$ are classified in Example 5.7. These are precisely the terms that appear in the ordinary cluster case.

#### Example 2.24.

Let $\ell_{2}=4$ and $\ell_{1}=1$ . We take the initial wall-functions

$$ P_{1}=\prod_{i=1}^{4}(1+s_{i}x)=1+p_{1,1}x+p_{1,2}x^{2}+p_{1,3}x^{3}+p_{1,4}x^{4}\quad\text{and}\quad P_{2}=1+p_{2,1}y. $$

The closed cone $C_{4,1}$ is a single ray $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(2,1)$ . The wall-function is again computed in [49] to be

$$ f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(2,1)}=\dfrac{\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq 4}(1+s_{i}s_{j}p_{2,1}x^{2}y)}{(1-p_{1,4}p_{2,1}^{2}x^{4}y^{2})^{4}}. $$

To simplify notations we let $x=y=p_{2,1}=1$ as they can be recovered from homogeneity constraints. We can rewrite

$$ \frac{\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq 4}(1+s_{i}s_{j})}{(1-p_{1,4})^{4}}=\frac{1+p_{1,2}+p_{1,4}}{(1-p_{1,4})^{2}}+\frac{(p_{1,1}p_{1,4}+p_{1,3})(p_{1,1}+p_{1,3})}{(1-p_{1,4})^{4}}. $$

The power series expansion of $f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(2,1)}$ then has nonnegative integer coefficients. Explicitly the expansion (with $x$ and $y$ omitted) is

$$ \sum_{k\geq 0}(2k+1)p_{1,4}^{k}p_{2,1}^{2k}+(k+1)p_{1,2}p_{1,4}^{k}p_{2,1}^{2k+1}+\binom{k+3}{3}p_{1,1}^{2}p_{1,4}^{k+1}p_{2,1}^{2k+3}\\
+\left[\binom{k+3}{3}+\binom{k+2}{3}\right]p_{1,1}p_{1,3}p_{1,4}^{k}p_{2,1}^{2k+2}+\binom{k+3}{3}p_{1,3}^{2}p_{1,4}^{k}p_{2,1}^{2k+3}. $$

A combinatorial interpretation of each term is given in Theorem 5.17. The objects corresponding to $(2k+1)p_{1,4}^{k}p_{2,1}^{2k}$ are classified in Example 5.8, which are precisely the terms that appear in the ordinary cluster case.

When $\ell_{1}\ell_{2}>4$ , the structure of $\mathfrak{D}$ within $C_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}$ is rather elusive. One aim of this paper is to understand the rays and their wall-functions within $C_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}$ . Theorem 5.17 in particular provides a combinatorial formula for the wall-function of every such ray. We further discuss in Appendix B that every ray within $C_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}$ is non-trivial and give a lower bound for wall-function coefficients.

### 2.3. Broken lines and theta functions

Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be a scattering diagram over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ as in Section 2.1.

#### Definition 2.26.

Let $m_{0}\in\mathscr{P}$ and $Q\in M_{\mathbb{R}}\cut\Supp(\mathfrak{D})$ . A broken line $\beta$ for $m_{0}$ with endpoint $Q$ is a piecewise linear continuous map

$$ \beta\colon(-\infty,0]\to M_{\mathbb{R}}\cut\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D}) $$

with values $-\infty=\tau_{0}<\tau_{1}<\cdots<\tau_{\ell+1}=0$ and an associated monomial $c_{i}x^{m_{i}}$ (with $c_{i}\in\Bbbk$ and $m_{i}\in\mathscr{P}$ ) for each domain of linearity $(\tau_{i},\tau_{i+1})$ , $i=0,\dots,\ell$ such that

- (1) $\beta(0)=Q$ and $c_{0}=1$ ;

- (2) $\dot{\beta}(\tau)=-r(m_{i})$ for any $\tau\in(\tau_{i},\tau_{i+1})$ for each $i=0,\dots,\ell$ ;

- (3) $\beta$ transversally crosses (the support of) some wall at $\tau_{i}$ for $i=1,\dots,\ell$ , that is, neither $-r(m_{i-1})$ nor $-r(m_{i})$ is tangent to the wall.

- (4) for $i=0,\dots,\ell-1$ , $c_{i+1}x^{m_{i+1}}$ is a monomial term (other than $c_{i}x^{m_{i}}$ ) of the power series

$$ c_{i}x^{m_{i}}\prod_{\{\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}\mid\beta(\tau_{i})\in S_{\mathfrak{d}}\}}f_{\mathfrak{d}}^{n_{i}\cdot r(m_{i})}, $$

where $n_{i}$ is primitive in $N$ and orthogonal to any $\mathfrak{d}$ with $\beta(\tau_{i})\in S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ such that $n_{i}\cdot r(m_{i})>0$ .

When $r(m_{0})=0$ , there is only the “static” broken line at $Q$ for $m_{0}$ and any endpoint $Q$ .

#### Definition 2.27.

The theta function associated to $m_{0}$ and $Q$ is

$$ \vartheta_{Q,m_{0}}\coloneqq\sum_{\beta}\operatorname{Mono}(\beta) $$

where the (formal) sum is over all broken lines for $m_{0}$ with endpoint $Q$ and $\operatorname{Mono}(\beta)=c_{\ell}x^{m_{\ell}}$ is the last monomial of $\beta$ .

#### Remark 2.28.

The theta function $\vartheta_{Q,m_{0}}$ can be viewed as an element in $x^{m_{0}}\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ . In fact, broken lines and theta functions can be defined for $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ . Then $\vartheta_{Q,m_{0}}$ is the limit of theta functions in $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ where each one is necessarily a finite sum in $x^{m_{0}}\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ . More detail is given in the proof of [27, Proposition 3.4].

#### Theorem 2.29 ([8], [27, Theorem 3.5]).

Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be a consistent scattering diagram, and let $m_{0}\in\mathscr{P}$ and $Q,Q^{\prime}\in M_{\mathbb{R}}\cut\operatorname{Supp}(\mathfrak{D})$ be two points. Suppose further that the coordinates of $Q$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ , and the same is true for $Q^{\prime}$ . Then for any regular path $\gamma$ with endpoints $\gamma(0)=Q$ and $\gamma(1)=Q^{\prime}$ , we have

$$ \vartheta_{Q^{\prime},m_{0}}=\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}(\vartheta_{Q,m_{0}}). $$

Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be $\Scat(P_{1},P_{2})$ as in Section 2.2. Define the weight of a broken line $\beta$ to be

$$ c(\beta)\coloneqq c_{\ell}x^{m_{\ell}}/x^{r(m_{\ell})}, $$

a monomial in $\Bbbk[\mathbb{M}]$ . Let $m(\beta)\coloneqq r(m_{\ell})$ . Thus $c(\beta)x^{m(\beta)}=\operatorname{Mono}(\beta)$ .

#### Corollary 2.31.

Let $m_{0}\in\mathscr{P}$ . For any $m_{\mathrm{fin}}\in M$ , the sum

$$ \sum_{m(\beta)=m_{\mathrm{fin}}}c(\beta)x^{m(\beta)} $$

over all broken lines $\beta$ for $m_{0}$ with endpoint $Q$ such that $m(\beta)=m_{\mathrm{fin}}$ is independent of $Q$ chosen generally in the same $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ . If $m_{\mathrm{fin}}$ is tangent to the ray $\mathcal{C}_{n}\cap\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ , then the sum is independent of $Q$ chosen generally in $\mathcal{C}_{n}\cup\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ .

#### Proof.

The first half is a direct corollary of Theorem 2.29. To see the second half, we choose general $Q\in\mathcal{C}_{n}$ , $Q^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ , and a regular path $\gamma$ with $\gamma(0)=Q$ and $\gamma(1)=Q^{\prime}$ . The path-ordered product $\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}$ is a single wall-crossing automorphism associated to the wall $\mathfrak{d}$ whose support is $\mathcal{C}_{n}\cap\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ . Then any monomial $x^{m^{\prime}}$ in the expansion of $\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}(x^{m})$ must have that $r(m^{\prime})=r(m)+km_{\mathfrak{d}}$ for some $k\in\mathbb{N}$ . In particular, $r(m^{\prime})$ is tangent to $\mathcal{C}_{n}\cap\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ if and only if $r(m)$ is. Then the result follows by comparing the monomials containing $x^{m}$ with $r(m)=m_{\mathrm{fin}}$ on the two sides of $\vartheta_{Q^{\prime},m_{0}}=\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}(\vartheta_{Q,m_{0}})$ . ∎

#### Proposition 2.32 (cf. [27, Proposition 3.6]).

The mutation $T$ in Theorem 2.16 defines a one-to-one correspondence $\beta\mapsto T(\beta)$ between broken lines for $m_{0}\in\mathscr{P}$ with endpoint $Q=(q_{1},q_{2})\in M_{\mathbb{R}}$ for $\mathfrak{D}=\Scat(P_{1},P_{2})$ and broken lines for $T(m_{0})$ with endpoint $T(Q)$ for $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}=\Scat(P_{1}^{\prime},P_{2})$ such that

$$ \operatorname{Mono}(T(\beta))=\begin{cases}T(\operatorname{Mono}(\beta))\quad&q_{2}\leq 0,\\
\operatorname{Mono}(\beta)\quad&q_{2}\geq 0.\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

One constructs the bijection in the same way as in the proof of [27, Proposition 3.6]. ∎

#### Proposition 2.33.

Let $m_{0}\in\mathcal{C}_{n}\cap M$ for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $Q$ be in the interior of $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ . Then

$$ \vartheta_{Q,m_{0}}=x^{m_{0}}. $$

#### Proof.

There is always the straight broken line without bending which contributes to $x^{m_{0}}$ in $\vartheta_{Q,m_{0}}$ . We need to show that this is the only broken line.

When $n=0$ , $\mathcal{C}_{0}$ is the first quadrant. For a broken line $\beta$ , if there is $t\in(-\infty,0)$ such that $\dot{\beta}(t)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}^{2}$ and $\beta(t)\notin\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{2}$ , then $\beta$ can never end at $Q$ in the interior of $\mathcal{C}_{0}$ . This is because $\beta$ can further bend only at the negative $x$ -axis, $y$ -axis, or the rays in the third quadrant. So $\dot{\beta}(t)$ (whenever defined) always stays in $\mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}^{2}$ and thus $\beta$ can never reach the first quadrant. Therefore we have proven the case $n=0$ .

For any other $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ , by applying Proposition 2.32 to a sequence of mutations we have a bijection between the broken lines for $m_{0}$ with endpoint $Q$ for $\mathfrak{D}$ and the broken lines for $T^{(n)}(m_{0})$ with endpoint $T^{(n)}(Q)$ for $\mathfrak{D}^{(n)}$ . Both $T^{(n)}(Q)$ and $T^{(n)}(m_{0})$ are in the positive chamber of $\mathfrak{D}^{(n)}$ . There is thus only one straight broken line by the case $n=0$ . It is pulled back to be the straight broken line $\beta$ in $\mathfrak{D}$ with $\operatorname{Mono}(\beta)=x^{m_{0}}$ . ∎

Let $Q_{+}$ denote a general point in the first quadrant $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{2}$ . It follows directly from Proposition 2.33 and Theorem 2.29 that for any $m$ in $\mathcal{C}_{n}\cap M$ ,

$$ \vartheta_{Q_{+},m}=\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}(x^{m}), $$

where $\gamma$ is a regular path from $Q\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{C}_{n})$ to $Q_{+}$ .

We now consider a sequence of theta functions known as cluster variables. This is an unorthodox way to introduce cluster variables, but it will soon be clear that they satisfy (generalized) cluster exchange relations [18, 9]. Denote $\vartheta_{m}=\vartheta_{Q_{+},m}$ .

#### Definition 2.35.

The cluster variables $\{x_{n}\mid n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ are defined to be

$$ x_{n}\coloneqq\vartheta_{-{\mathbf{d}}_{n}}. $$

#### Lemma 2.36.

The cluster variables satisfy the following cluster exchange relations

- (1) $x_{0}x_{2}=P_{1}(x_{1})$ ,

- (2) $x_{1}x_{3}=P_{2}(x_{2})$ ,

- (3) $x_{n-1}x_{n+1}=\bar{\zeta}_{n}(x_{n})$ for $n\neq 1,2$ ,

where $\bar{\zeta}_{n}(z)\coloneqq z^{\deg(\zeta_{n})}\zeta_{n}(1/z)$ .

#### Proof.

We first check (1) and (2). By Proposition 2.33, we have $x_{1}=x$ and $x_{2}=y$ . Notice $x_{0}=\vartheta_{(0,-1)}$ and $x_{3}=\vartheta_{(-1,0)}$ . By (2.34), we have $x_{0}=x_{2}^{-1}P_{1}(x_{1})$ and $x_{3}=x_{1}^{-1}P_{2}(x_{2})$ .

For any $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ , let $\gamma_{n}$ be a regular path going from the interior of $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ to the first quadrant $\mathcal{C}_{0}$ . For some $n\neq 1,2$ , let $\gamma$ be a regular path going from $\mathcal{C}_{n-1}$ to $\mathcal{C}_{n-2}$ by crossing the wall $(\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}d_{n},\zeta_{n})$ . Then we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}(x^{-d_{1;n+1}}y^{-d_{2;n+1}}) \displaystyle=x^{-d_{1;n+1}}y^{-d_{2;n+1}}\zeta_{n}(x^{d_{1;n}}y^{d_{2;n}}) \displaystyle=x^{\deg(\zeta_{n})d_{1;n}-d_{1;n+1}}y^{\deg(\zeta_{n})d_{2;n}-d_{2;n+1}}\bar{\zeta}_{n}(x^{-d_{1;n}}y^{-d_{2;n}}) \displaystyle=x^{d_{1;n-1}}y^{d_{2;n-1}}\bar{\zeta}_{n}(x^{-d_{1;n}}y^{-d_{2;n}}). $$

Applying $\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma_{n-2},\mathfrak{D}}$ to both sides of the above equation, we obtain

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{\gamma_{n-1},\mathfrak{D}}\left(x^{-d_{1;n+1}}y^{-d_{2;n+1}}\right)=\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma_{n-2},\mathfrak{D}}\left(x^{d_{1;n-1}}y^{d_{2;n-1}}\right)\bar{\zeta}_{n}\left(\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma_{n-2},\mathfrak{D}}\left(x^{-d_{1;n}}y^{-d_{2;n}}\right)\right). $$

Now by (2.34), we have for $n\geq 3$ ,

$$ x_{n+1}=x_{n-1}^{-1}\bar{\zeta}_{n}(x_{n}).\qed $$

### 2.4. Theta functions are universal Laurent

Recall the notations in Section 2.2. In that situation the monoid $\mathscr{P}$ decomposes as $M\oplus\mathbb{M}$ , where $\mathbb{M}=\mathbb{M}_{1}\oplus\mathbb{M}_{2}$ embeds in $\mathbb{P}$ the group of Laurent monomials in $\{p_{i,j}\mid i=1,2,1\leq j\leq\ell_{i}\}$ . Elements in $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ are regarded as coefficients.

Let $\mathcal{F}$ denote the field of rational functions $\operatorname{Frac}(\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}])$ . The generalized cluster algebra $\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}(P_{1},P_{2})$ is defined to be the $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ -subalgebra in $\mathcal{F}$ generated by all cluster variables $\{x_{n}\mid n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ . The generalized upper cluster algebra is defined to be

$$ \mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}(P_{1},P_{2})\coloneqq\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{n}^{\pm 1},x_{n+1}^{\pm 1}]\subseteq\mathcal{F}. $$

An element in $\mathcal{U}$ is called universal Laurent as it belongs to every $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{n}^{\pm 1},x_{n+1}^{\pm 1}]$ .

#### Proposition 2.38.

For any $m\in M$ , the theta function $\vartheta_{m}$ belongs to ${\mathcal{U}}$ . Hence $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{U}$ .

#### Proof.

This is a slight generalization from [10, Theorem 3.9(b)(c)] to our setting. For each $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ , choose a general point $Q_{n}$ in its interior. If $m\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ , we have $\vartheta_{m}=\vartheta_{Q_{0},m}=x^{m}$ by Proposition 2.33. If $m\notin\mathbb{N}^{2}$ , for any broken line $\beta$ for $m$ with endpoint $Q_{0}$ , the vector $m_{\beta}\in M=\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ has at least one negative coordinate. Then there are finitely many walls where any such $\beta$ can bend. Moreover only finitely many terms on these wall-functions are relevant. Then $\vartheta_{m}$ can be equivalently computed in $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ for a large $k$ . Therefore, $\vartheta_{m}$ is a Laurent monomials. This shows $\vartheta_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{1}^{\pm 1},x_{2}^{\pm 1}]$ for any $m\in M$ .

For any $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ , we first show that $\vartheta_{Q_{n},m}$ is in $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{1}^{\pm 1},x_{2}^{\pm 1}]$ . By Proposition 2.32, there is a piecewise linear transformation $T^{(n)}\colon M_{\mathbb{R}}\rightarrow M_{\mathbb{R}}$ that takes $\mathcal{C}_{n}$ to the positive chamber of $\mathfrak{D}^{(n)}$ , which induces a one-to-one correspondence between broken lines in $\mathfrak{D}$ and those in $\mathfrak{D}^{(n)}$ . Since $T^{(n)}(Q_{n})$ lies in the positive chamber of $\mathfrak{D}^{(n)}$ , there are finitely many broken lines by the first paragraph. Thus there are too only finitely many broken lines for $\vartheta_{Q_{n},m}$ , which means $\vartheta_{Q_{n},m}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{1}^{\pm 1},x_{2}^{\pm 1}]$ .

Each cluster variable $x_{n}$ corresponds to the ray $\mathcal{C}_{n-2}\cap\mathcal{C}_{n-1}$ in the cluster complex. The primitive integral generator of this ray is $-{\mathbf{d}}_{n}$ (see Definition 2.35). Any pair $\{{\mathbf{d}}_{n},{\mathbf{d}}_{n+1}\}$ is a basis of $M$ (Lemma 2.19). Then for any $m\in M$ we have

$$ \vartheta_{Q_{n},m}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x^{\pm{\mathbf{d}}_{n+1}},x^{\pm{\mathbf{d}}_{n+2}}]. $$

Therefore for a regular path $\gamma$ from $Q_{n}$ to $Q_{0}$ , we have by Theorem 2.29 that

$$ \vartheta_{m}=\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}(\vartheta_{Q_{n},m})\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{n+1}^{\pm 1},x_{n+2}^{\pm 1}].\qed $$

#### Definition 2.39.

The set of theta functions $\{\vartheta_{m}\mid m\in M\}$ is called the generalized theta basis of $\mathcal{U}$ .

#### Remark 2.40.

One can prove that theta functions $\{\vartheta_{m}\mid m\in M\}$ form a $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ -basis of $\mathcal{U}$ analogously as in [27]. This also follows from the fact that theta functions equal so-called greedy elements, proven in Section 4, and that the greedy elements form a basis of $\mathcal{U}$ .

## 3. Greedy bases for rank-2 generalized cluster algebras

Following Lee–Li–Zelevinsky [36] in the cluster algebra setting and Rupel [51] in the palindromic generalized cluster algebra setting, we define the generalized greedy basis for rank- $2$ generalized cluster algebras. We will then, following these previous works, show that the coefficients can be realized as counts of combinatorial objects called compatible gradings.

### 3.1. Generalized greedy elements

Let $\mathcal{T}_{k}=\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{k}^{\pm 1},x_{k+1}^{\pm 1}]$ for $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Therefore $\mathcal{U}=\bigcap_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{T}_{k}$ from (2.37).

#### Definition 3.1.

An element $x\in\mathcal{T}_{k}$ is pointed at $(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ in the $k^{\text{th}}$ cluster if it can be expressed in the form

$$ x=x_{k}^{-d_{1}}x_{k+1}^{-d_{2}}\sum_{p,q\geq 0}c(p,q)x_{k}^{p}x_{k+1}^{q} $$

for some $c(p,q)\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ and $c(0,0)=1$ .

An element pointed in the initial cluster $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ is simply called pointed.

#### Definition 3.2.

For a sequence of variables $p_{\bullet}=(p_{k})_{k=1}^{\ell}$ where $\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\cup\{\infty\}$ with $\deg p_{k}=k$ , we write for any $m\geq 0$

$$ \left(1+\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{k}x^{k}\right)^{m}=\sum_{n\geq 0}\pi_{m,n}(p_{\bullet})x^{n}, $$

defining $\pi_{m,n}(p_{\bullet})$ as a homogeneous polynomial in $(p_{k})_{k}$ of degree $n$ . We write for $m\geq 0$

$$ \left(1+\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{k}x^{k}\right)^{-m}=\sum_{n\geq 0}\varsigma_{m,n}(p_{\bullet})x^{n}, $$

defining $\varsigma_{m,n}(p_{\bullet})$ as a homogeneous polynomial in $(p_{k})_{k}$ of degree $n$ .

We take the conventions that $\pi_{m,0}(p_{\bullet})=\varsigma_{m,0}(p_{\bullet})=1$ for any $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ and that $\pi_{m,n}(p_{\bullet})=\varsigma_{m,n}(p_{\bullet})=0$ when $m<0$ and $n\neq 0$ .

#### Lemma 3.3.

For any $s\geq 1$

$$ \sum_{k=0}^{s}\pi_{m,s-k}(p_{\bullet})\varsigma_{m,k}(p_{\bullet})=0. $$

#### Proof.

By Definition 3.2, we have $\left(\sum_{n\geq 0}\pi_{m,n}(p_{\bullet})x^{n}\right)\left(\sum_{n\geq 0}\varsigma_{m,n}(p_{\bullet})x^{n}\right)=1$ . The statement then follows from isolating the $s^{\text{th}}$ coefficient of this product. ∎

The above lemma implies

$$ \pi_{m,s}(p_{\bullet})=\sum_{k=1}^{s}-\pi_{m,s-k}(p_{\bullet})\varsigma_{m,k}(p_{\bullet}). $$

This can be seen as a recursive definition of $\pi_{m,s}(p_{\bullet})$ for $m,s\geq 1$ . The fact that any $\pi_{m,s}(p_{\bullet})$ has nonnegative integer coefficients is less obvious from this definition. Next we consider a two-dimensional recursion generalizing (3.4).

For an element $f$ in any polynomial ring $Y=\mathbb{Z}[y_{1},...,y_{n}]$ where $y_{1},...,y_{n}$ are algebraically independent, and for $e=(e_{1},...,e_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{n}$ , let $[y^{e}]f=[y_{1}^{e_{1}}\cdots y_{n}^{e_{n}}]f$ be the coefficient of $y_{1}^{e_{1}}\cdots y_{n}^{e_{n}}$ in $f$ . For a pair of elements $f$ and $g$ in $Y$ , we define

$$ \operatorname{T-max}(f,g)\coloneqq\sum_{e\in\mathbb{N}^{n}}\max([y^{e}]f,[y^{e}]g)y^{e}. $$

Consider two sequences of variables $p_{i,\bullet}=(p_{i,k})_{k=1}^{\ell_{i}}$ for $i=1,2$ and $\ell_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\cup\{\infty\}$ .

#### Definition 3.5.

Fix $(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ . Define $c(p,q)\in\mathbb{Z}[p_{1,\bullet}\cup p_{2,\bullet}]$ for any $(p,q)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ by the base case $c(0,0)=1$ and the recursion

$$ c(p,q)\coloneqq\operatorname{T-max}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{p}-c(p-k,q)\varsigma_{d_{2}-q,k}(p_{1,\bullet}),\ \sum_{k=1}^{q}-c(p,q-k)\varsigma_{d_{1}-p,k}(p_{2,\bullet})\right). $$

#### Remark 3.6.

It is not hard to determine all $c(p,q)$ unless both $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ are positive. In fact, we have by (3.4) that

- (1) when $d_{1}\leq 0,d_{2}\leq 0$ , every $c(p,q)=0$ except $c(0,0)=1$ ;

- (2) when $d_{1}\leq 0,d_{2}\geq 0$ , every $c(p,q)=0$ except $c(p,0)=\pi_{d_{2},p}(p_{1,\bullet})$ ;

- (3) when $d_{1}\geq 0,d_{2}\leq 0$ , every $c(p,q)=0$ except $c(0,q)=\pi_{d_{1},q}(p_{2,\bullet})$ .

#### Definition 3.7.

Define $d_{+}(0,0)=d_{-}(0,0)\coloneqq c(0,0)=1$ , and for $(p,q)\neq(0,0)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle d_{+}(p,q)\coloneqq c(p,q)-\sum_{k=1}^{p}-c(p-k,q)\varsigma_{d_{2}-q,k}(p_{1,\bullet}), \displaystyle d_{-}(p,q)\coloneqq c(p,q)-\sum_{k=1}^{q}-c(p,q-k)\varsigma_{d_{1}-p,k}(p_{2,\bullet}). $$

By definition, both $d_{\pm}(p,q)$ are polynomials with nonnegative integer coefficients.

#### Lemma 3.8.

We have

$$ \displaystyle c(p,q) \displaystyle=d_{+}(p,q)+\sum_{s=1}^{p}\pi_{d_{2}-q,s}(p_{1,\bullet})d_{+}(p-s,q) \displaystyle=d_{-}(p,q)+\sum_{s=1}^{q}\pi_{d_{1}-p,s}(p_{2,\bullet})d_{-}(p,q-s). $$

#### Proof.

We prove the first equality by induction on $p$ . By the definition of $d_{+}(p,q)$ , it is equivalent to show

$$ \sum_{k=1}^{p}-c(p-k,q)\varsigma_{d_{2}-q,k}(p_{1,\bullet})=\sum_{s=1}^{p}\pi_{d_{2}-q,s}(p_{1,\bullet})d_{+}(p-s,q). $$

We only need to deal with the case when $d_{2}-q\geq 1$ . Assume that the first equality is true for $c(0,q),\dots,c(p-1,q)$ . Then we can write the left-hand side of (3.9) as

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{p}-\varsigma_{d_{2}-q,k}(p_{1,\bullet})\sum_{t=0}^{p-k}\pi_{d_{2}-q,t}(p_{1,\bullet})d_{+}(p-k-t,q) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{s=1}^{p}d_{+}(p-s,q)\sum_{k=1}^{s}-\pi_{d_{2}-q,s-k}(p_{1,\bullet})\varsigma_{d_{2}-q,k}(p_{1,\bullet}). $$

Applying (3.4), the above equals the right-hand side of (3.9).

The second equality of the statement can be proven similarly by induction on $q$ . ∎

A consequence of Lemma 3.8 is that each $c(p,q)$ has nonnegative integer coefficients.

#### Definition 3.10.

For $(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ , we define the greedy element

$$ x[d_{1},d_{2}]\coloneqq x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\sum_{(p,q)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}}c(p,q)x_{1}^{p}x_{2}^{q}\in x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\mathbb{N}[p_{1,\bullet}\cup p_{2,\bullet}]\llbracket x_{1},x_{2}\rrbracket. $$

According to Remark 3.6, the greedy elements are clear in the following cases

$$ x[d_{1},d_{2}]=\begin{cases}x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\quad&d_{1}\leq 0,d_{2}\leq 0,\\
x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\left(1+\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{1,k}x_{1}^{k}\right)^{d_{1}}\quad&d_{1}\geq 0,d_{2}\leq 0,\\
x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\left(1+\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{2,k}x_{2}^{k}\right)^{d_{2}}\quad&d_{1}\leq 0,d_{2}\geq 0.\end{cases} $$

When $p_{1,\bullet}$ and $p_{2,\bullet}$ are both finite sequences, in the cases of (3.11), $x[d_{1},d_{2}]$ is a finite sum, thus a pointed element in $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ (Definition 3.1). When $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ are positive, $x[d_{1},d_{2}]$ is also a finite sum. This fact is non-trivial from the definition and is a consequence of the combinatorial formula of $x[d_{1},d_{2}]$ given in Theorem 3.18, where each $c(p,q)$ is interpreted as the weighted count of combinatorial objects called compatible gradings.

### 3.2. Compatible gradings

#### Definition 3.12.

A North-East (NE) path $\mathcal{P}$ is a lattice path in $(\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{R})\cup(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z})\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}$ starting at $(0,0)$ and ending at $(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ , proceeding by only unit north and east steps. We also view $\mathcal{P}$ as the set of its unit north and east steps, where we refer to each step as an edge.

- • Given a set $C$ of edges in $\mathcal{P}$ , we denote the set of horizontal edges (east steps) by $C_{\mathbf{E}}$ and the set of vertical edges (north steps) by $C_{\mathbf{N}}$ . We let $|C|$ denote the number of edges in $C$ .

- • For edges $e$ and $f$ in $\mathcal{P}$ , let $\overrightarrow{ef}$ denote the subpath proceeding east from $e$ to $f$ (including both $e$ and $f$ ), continuing cyclically around $\mathcal{P}$ if $e$ is to the north or east of $f$ .

Note that if $e=f$ , then $\overrightarrow{ef}=\{e\}$ . If $e$ is the edge adjacent to $f$ and to the northeast of $f$ , then $\overrightarrow{ef}=\mathcal{P}$ .

Consider the rectangle $R(d_{1},d_{2})$ with vertices $(0,0)$ , $(0,d_{2})$ , $(d_{1},0)$ , and $(d_{1},d_{2})$ with a main diagonal from $(0,0)$ to $(d_{1},d_{2})$ . A Dyck path is an NE path from $(0,0)$ to $(d_{1},d_{2})$ that never passes strictly above the main diagonal of $R(d_{1},d_{2})$ . The Dyck paths from $(0,0)$ to $(d_{1},d_{2})$ form a partially ordered set by comparing the heights at all vertices. The maximal Dyck path $\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2})$ is the maximal element under this partial order. When $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ are relatively prime, the maximal Dyck path $\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2})$ corresponds to the lower Christoffel word of slope $d_{2}/d_{1}$ . We label the horizontal edges from left to right by $u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{d_{1}}$ and the vertical edges from bottom to top by $v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{d_{2}}$ .

#### Example 3.13.

In Figure 2, the maximal Dyck path $\mathcal{P}(6,4)$ is shown in the top left and $\mathcal{P}(7,4)$ is shown in the top right.

Motivated by Lee–Schiffler [37], Lee, Li, and Zelevinsky [36] introduced combinatorial objects called compatible pairs to construct the greedy basis for rank- $2$ cluster algebras, consisting of indecomposable positive elements including the cluster monomials. Rupel [51, 52] extended this construction to the setting of generalized rank- $2$ cluster algebras by defining compatible gradings.

A grading $\omega:\mathcal{P}\to\mathbb{N}$ assigns a nonnegative integer to every edge of the NE path $\mathcal{P}$ . For any grading $\omega$ and for any set of edges $C\subseteq\mathcal{P}$ , let $\displaystyle\omega(C)\coloneqq\sum_{e\in C}\omega(e)$ .

#### Definition 3.14.

Let $\mathcal{P}$ be an NE path. A grading $\omega:\mathcal{P}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ is called compatible if for every pair of $u\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}}$ and $v\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}}$ with $\omega(u)\omega(v)>0$ , there exists an edge $e$ along the subpath $\overrightarrow{uv}$ so that at least one of the following holds:

$$ \displaystyle e\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}}\setminus\{v\}\quad\text{and}\quad|\overrightarrow{ue}_{\mathbf{N}}|=\omega\left(\overrightarrow{ue}_{\mathbf{E}}\right); \displaystyle e\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}}\setminus\{u\}\quad\text{and}\quad|\overrightarrow{ev}_{\mathbf{E}}|=\omega\left(\overrightarrow{ev}_{\mathbf{N}}\right). $$

#### Example 3.16.

For each $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ , let $\omega_{i}:\mathcal{P}(i+5,4)\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ be the grading given by $\omega_{i}(u_{1})=\omega_{i}(u_{2})=2$ , $\omega_{i}(v_{3})=\omega_{i}(v_{4})=3$ , and $\omega_{i}(e)=0$ for every edge $e$ in $\mathcal{P}(i+5,4)\setminus\{u_{1},u_{2},v_{3},v_{4}\}$ (see Figure 2 for $i=1,2$ ). Then $\omega_{1}$ is not compatible, but $\omega_{2}$ and $\omega_{3}$ are compatible. The main difference between $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ is that the edge $e=u_{2}$ in $\mathcal{P}(7,4)$ satisfies the second condition in (3.15) for $u=u_{1}$ and $v=v_{4}$ , as both sides of the equation equal $6$ .

### 3.3. Generalized greedy element formula

We now give a combinatorial interpretation of the coefficients of generalized greedy elements using compatible gradings, as presented in Theorem 3.18. This generalizes the work of Rupel [50, Theorem 2.15] to the non-palindromic setting, which will be needed in our discussion on the positivity of higher-rank scattering diagrams in Section 9. The proof of Theorem 3.18, which is inspired by Rupel’s work, will be given in Appendix A.

Let $\mathbb{M}$ denote the multiplicative monoid of monomials in $p_{1,\bullet}\cup p_{2,\bullet}$ .

#### Definition 3.17.

The weight of a grading $\omega:\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2})\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ is the monomial

$$ \text{wt}(\omega)\coloneqq\prod_{i=1}^{d_{1}}p_{2,\omega(u_{i})}\prod_{j=1}^{d_{2}}p_{1,\omega(v_{j})}\in\mathbb{M}\,. $$

Fix $(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ . Let $\CG(d_{1},d_{2},p,q)=\CG(p,q)$ denote the set of all compatible gradings $\omega$ on $\mathcal{P}([d_{1}]_{+},[d_{2}]_{+})$ such that $\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})=q$ and $\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})=p$ . Define the weighted sum

$$ |\CG(p,q)|\coloneqq\sum_{\omega\in\CG(p,q)}\text{wt}(\omega)\in\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{M}]\,. $$

The coefficients $c(p,q)$ of a generalized greedy element are then given as weighted sums of compatible gradings on a fixed Dyck path with a fixed total vertical and horizontal grading.

#### Theorem 3.18.

For any $(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ , the greedy element $x[d_{1},d_{2}]$ can be computed as

$$ x[d_{1},d_{2}]=x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\sum_{\omega}\wt(\omega)x_{1}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})}x_{2}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})}\,, $$

where the sum is over all compatible gradings $\omega$ on $\mathcal{P}([d_{1}]_{+},[d_{2}]_{+})$ . In other words, for any $(p,q)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ , we have

$$ c(p,q)=|\CG(p,q)|\,. $$

When $\ell_{1},\ell_{2}<\infty$ , we set in Definition 3.17 that $p_{1,k}=0$ for any $k>\ell_{1}$ and $p_{2,k}=0$ for any $k>\ell_{2}$ . Then in this case, it follows from (3.19) that $x[d_{1},d_{2}]$ is always a finite sum as there are only finitely many gradings with non-zero weights.

We will show in Corollary A.10 that $x[d_{1},d_{2}]$ is not only a pointed element in $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ , but also belongs to any other $\mathcal{T}_{k}$ (hence in $\mathcal{U}$ which actually equals $\mathcal{A}(P_{1},P_{2})$ ). Moreover, the set of all greedy elements

$$ \{x[d_{1},d_{2}]\mid(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\} $$

is in fact a $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ -basis of $\mathcal{A}(P_{1},P_{2})$ . This statement generalizes [36, Theorem 1.7(c)] and can be proven analogously as in [36, Section 6]. This basis will be referred to as the generalized greedy basis.

## 4. The generalized greedy basis equals the generalized theta basis

It was shown by Cheung, Gross, Muller, Musiker, Rupel, Stella, and Williams that, in the setting of cluster algebras, the greedy basis equals the theta basis [10]. Their proof is algebraic, using a characterization of greedy elements by their support and properties of rank- $2$ scattering diagrams. We extend their results to the generalized setting.

#### Theorem 4.1.

The generalized greedy basis equals the generalized theta basis. More precisely, $\vartheta_{-(d_{1},d_{2})}=x[d_{1},d_{2}]$ for any $(d_{1},d_{2})\in M$ .

Before presenting the proof, we establish a couple of lemmas. First, we give a support condition that can be used to identify generalized greedy elements, following [10, Scholium 2.6]. A crucial part of this argument is the compatible grading formula for coefficients of generalized greedy elements, which is developed in the previous section (see Theorem 3.18).

#### Definition 4.2.

Let $R^{\circ}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ be a region in $M_{\mathbb{R}}=\mathbb{R}^{2}$ defined as follows:

- (1) If $d_{1},d_{2}\leq 0$ , then $R^{\circ}_{d_{1},d_{2}}=\{(-d_{1},-d_{2})\}$ ,

- (2) If $d_{1}\leq 0<d_{2}$ , then $R^{\circ}_{d_{1},d_{2}}=\{(m_{1},-d_{2}):-d_{1}\leq m_{1}\leq-d_{1}+\ell_{1}d_{2}\}$ ,

- (3) If $d_{2}\leq 0<d_{1}$ , then $R^{\circ}_{d_{1},d_{2}}=\{(-d_{1},m_{2}):-d_{2}\leq m_{2}\leq-d_{2}+\ell_{2}d_{1}\}$ ,

- (4) Otherwise, consider the vertices $O=(0,0)$ , $A=(-d_{1}+\ell_{1}d_{2},-d_{2})$ , $B=(-d_{1},-d_{2})$ , and $C=(-d_{1},-d_{2}+\ell_{2}d_{1})$ . Then $R^{\circ}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ is the interior of the polygon $OABC$ along with the closed line segments $AB$ and $BC$ (see [10, Figure 1]).

Given a Laurent polynomial $f=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}}c_{m}x^{m}$ in $\Bbbk[\mathbb{Z}^{\ell_{1}}\oplus\mathbb{Z}^{\ell_{2}}][x_{1}^{\pm 1},x_{2}^{\pm 1}]$ , the support of $f$ is the set $\{m\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}:c_{m}\neq 0\}$ . Rupel showed that the region $R^{\circ}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ contains the support of the generalized greedy element $x[d_{1},d_{2}]$ when $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ satisfy certain restrictions. In fact, this result also holds with these restrictions removed.

#### Proposition 4.3 ([51, Proposition 4.22]).

The support of the generalized greedy element $x[d_{1},d_{2}]$ is contained in $R^{\circ}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ .

#### Proof.

Rupel showed that this holds when $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are palindromic polynomials by considering the generalized greedy coefficients as counts of compatible gradings ([51, Theorem 2.15]). In the previous section, we extend this interpretation to the non-palindromic setting (see Theorem 3.18). Rupel’s argument then also holds without requiring $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ to be palindromic. ∎

We then obtain the following characterization of generalized greedy elements.

#### Lemma 4.4 ([10, Scholium 2.6]).

If $z\in\mathcal{A}(P_{1},P_{2})$ is any element containing the monomial $x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}$ with coefficient $1$ and whose support is contained in $R^{\circ}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ , then $z=x[d_{1},d_{2}]$ .

#### Proof.

This follows directly from the proof of [10, Theorem 2.5] and the proof of [10, Scholium 2.6], both of which carry through in the generalized cluster algebra setting. ∎

Thus, it is enough to show that the support of each generalized theta basis element is contained in $R^{\circ}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ for a corresponding choice of $d_{1},d_{2}$ . This is shown in the classical setting in [10, Section 5], and their methods work essentially verbatim in the generalized case. Their results do not rely on the structure of the scattering diagram, other than that all walls are along the coordinate axes or in the third quadrant, which holds for the generalized cluster scattering diagrams. This culminates in bounds on the final exponent of the broken lines contributing to the generalized theta basis, yielding the desired bounds on the support of the theta basis elements.

#### Definition 4.5.

Given a broken line $\beta$ , fix a point $q=(q_{1},q_{2})\in M_{\mathbb{R}}$ on the linear portion $\beta|_{(\tau_{i-1},\tau_{i})}$ . The angular momentum of $\beta$ (at $q$ ) is given by the dot product $(q_{2},-q_{1})\cdot r(m_{i})$ .

The angular momentum of a broken line does not depend on the choice of $q$ , as shown in [10, Lemma 5.3]. Broken lines of positive (resp. negative) angular momentum proceed counter-clockwise (resp. clockwise) around the origin. The behavior of broken lines terminating in the first quadrant can be characterized based on the sign of their angular momentum [10, Lemma 5.4]. If $\beta$ is a broken line of positive (resp. negative) angular momentum, then the slopes of the linear domains of $\beta$ decrease (resp. increase) at each bend, except possibly at the boundary of the first quadrant.

Fix a general point $Q_{+}$ in the first quadrant of $M_{\mathbb{R}}=\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , and denote $\vartheta_{Q_{+},m}=\vartheta_{m}$ for $m\in M$ .

#### Lemma 4.6 ([10, Lemma 5.5]).

Let $\gamma$ be a broken line in $\Scat(P_{1},P_{2})$ which begins in the third quadrant, with endpoint $Q_{+}$ in the first quadrant. Denote the initial exponent by $(-d_{1},-d_{2})$ and the final exponent by $m(\gamma)=(m_{1},m_{2})$ .

- (1) If $\gamma$ has positive angular momentum, then $-d_{2}\leq m_{2}<0$ and

$$ -d_{1}\leq m_{1}\leq\left(\frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}-\ell_{1}\right)m_{2}\,, $$

where the upper bound is achieved only when $(m_{1},m_{2})=(-d_{1}+\ell_{1}d_{2},-d_{2})$ .

- (2) If $\gamma$ has negative angular momentum, then $-d_{1}\leq m_{1}<0$ and

$$ -d_{2}\leq m_{2}\leq\left(\frac{d_{2}}{d_{1}}-\ell_{2}\right)m_{1}\,, $$

where the upper bound is achieved only when $(m_{1},m_{2})=(-d_{1},-d_{2}+\ell_{2}d_{1})$ .

We now have all the tools necessary to prove Theorem 4.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 4.1.

We proceed by showing that the theta function $\vartheta_{(-d_{1},-d_{2})}$ satisfies the conditions of Lemma 4.4, following the approach of [10, Proof of Theorem 5.1]. First, note that a broken line with the same initial and terminal momentum in $\Scat(P_{1},P_{2})$ must not bend, as any bending would increase one of the entries of the exponent. There is a unique broken line terminating at $Q_{+}$ that does not bend and has terminal momentum $(-d_{1},-d_{2})$ , which contributes the term $x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}$ to $\vartheta_{(-d_{1},-d_{2})}$ . Hence $x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}$ appears with coefficient $1$ in $\vartheta_{(-d_{1},-d_{2})}$ . For the support condition, we split into four cases.

- (1) If $d_{1},d_{2}\leq 0$ , then by Proposition 2.33 we have $\vartheta_{(-d_{1},-d_{2})}=x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}$ , so the support is simply $\{(-d_{1},-d_{2})\}=R^{\circ}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ .

- (2) If $d_{1}\leq 0<d_{2}$ , then a broken line with initial momentum $(-d_{1},-d_{2})$ terminating at $Q_{+}$ can bend only at the $x$ -axis. This follows because any other bending would need to occur to the left of $Q_{+}$ , and such a broken line can never move in the positive $x$ direction to return to $Q_{+}$ . Thus, the terminal momentums of broken lines that contribute to $\vartheta_{(-d_{1},-d_{2})}$ are precisely $(-d_{1},-d_{2})+i(\ell_{1},0)$ for any integer $i\in\{0,1,\dots,\ell_{1}\}$ .

- (3) If $d_{2}\leq 0<d_{1}$ , then an analogous argument to that in Case (2) applies.

- (4) If $d_{1},d_{2}>0$ , then we can apply Lemma 4.6 to conclude that the final exponent of any broken line $\gamma$ contributing to $\vartheta_{(-d_{1},-d_{2})}$ must have final exponent contained in $R^{\circ}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ .

Therefore, the terminal momentum of any broken line contributing to $\vartheta_{(-d_{1},-d_{2})}$ , and hence the support of $\vartheta_{(-d_{1},-d_{2})}$ , is contained in $R^{\circ}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ . Applying Lemma 4.4, we can conclude that $\vartheta_{(-d_{1},-d_{2})}=x[d_{1},d_{2}]$ . ∎

## 5. Shadowed gradings and tight gradings

We define new combinatorial objects called tight gradings that give a combinatorial interpretation of the wall-function coefficients in rank- $2$ generalized cluster scattering diagrams. By considering a larger class of gradings called shadowed gradings, we also give a combinatorial interpretation of the coefficients of powers of the wall-functions. The latter is useful for computing Euler characteristics of quiver moduli (see Section 6.1) and relative Gromov–Witten invariant in toric surfaces (see Section 6.2).

In this section, we begin by defining shadowed gradings and tight gradings. We then describe certain conditions under which we can isolate a unique broken line that corresponds to a set of shadowed gradings. Utilizing these conditions, we relate the combinatorial approach of Lee–Li–Zelevinsky and the scattering diagram approach of Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich [36, 27]. This yields a directly computable, manifestly positive, and elementary but highly nontrivial formula describing rank-2 consistent scattering diagrams.

### 5.1. Shadowed gradings and tight gradings

We now introduce shadowed gradings and tight gradings, which are subsets of the compatible gradings defined by Rupel [51] and inspired by the compatible pairs of Lee–Li–Zelevinsky [36] (see Section 3.2). We first require the notion of the “shadow” of a set of edges in an NE path.

#### Definition 5.1.

Fix an NE path $\mathcal{P}$ and a grading $\omega\colon\mathcal{P}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ . For each edge $e$ in $\mathcal{P}$ , we define its shadow, denoted by $\sh(e)$ or $\sh(e;\omega)$ , as follows.

- • If $e$ is horizontal, then its shadow is $(\overrightarrow{ev})_{\mathbf{N}}$ , where $v\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}}$ is chosen such that $|(\overrightarrow{ev})_{\mathbf{N}}|=\omega((\overrightarrow{ev})_{\mathbf{E}})$ and $\overrightarrow{ev}$ has minimal length under this condition. If no such $v$ exists, let $\sh(e)=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}}$ .

- • If $e$ is vertical, then its shadow is $(\overrightarrow{ue})_{\mathbf{E}}$ , where $u\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}}$ is chosen such that $|(\overrightarrow{ue})_{\mathbf{E}}|=\omega((\overrightarrow{ue})_{\mathbf{N}})$ and $\overrightarrow{ue}$ has minimal length under this condition. If no such $u$ exists, let $\sh(e)=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}}$ .

For $S\subset\mathcal{P}$ , let the shadow of $S$ be $\sh(S)=\bigcup_{e\in S}\sh(e)$ .

Note that if $\omega(e)=0$ , then $\sh(e)=\emptyset$ .

#### Example 5.2.

Consider $\omega_{2}$ as in Example 3.16. Then $\sh(u_{2})=\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$ and $\sh(u_{1})=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{4}\}=\sh(\{u_{1},u_{2}\})$ . We also have $\sh(v_{3})=\{u_{4},u_{5},u_{6}\}$ and $\sh(v_{4})=\{u_{2},u_{3},\dots,u_{7}\}=\sh(\{v_{3},v_{4}\})$ .

We then define a subset of compatible gradings where the vertical edges with nonzero grading value are contained in the shadow of the horizontal edges, or vice versa.

#### Definition 5.3.

A shadowed grading on $\mathcal{P}$ is a compatible grading satisfying either

$$ S_{\mathbf{E}}\subseteq\sh(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})\quad\text{or}\quad S_{\mathbf{N}}\subseteq\sh(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})\,, $$

where $S$ is the set of edges $e$ in $\mathcal{P}$ with $\omega(e)>0$ .

The notion of shadowed gradings generalizes the notion of tight gradings, as first defined in [7] and partially motivated by [6].

#### Definition 5.4.

Let $\omega$ be a grading on $\mathcal{P}$ with $p=\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})$ and $q=\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})$ . The grading $\omega$ is a tight grading if $\omega$ is a shadowed grading satisfying $p\leq d_{1}$ , $q\leq d_{2}$ , and

$$ pd_{2}-qd_{1}=\pm\gcd(p,q)\,. $$

We now explain how to represent shadowed gradings as rectangular tilings. This is important for the illustration of shadowed and tight gradings. First, rotate (i.e. cyclically shift) the maximal Dyck path so that the shadow of each horizontal (resp. vertical) edge does not extend beyond the left (resp. top) boundary of the rotated path. Such a rotation always exists provided $\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})\leq d_{1}$ and $\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})\leq d_{2}$ , which always holds for tight gradings. Then draw blue rectangles above each horizontal edge $e$ with total height equal to $|\sh(e)|$ , partitioned into the vertical grading values contributing to the shadow. Similarly, we draw red rectangles to the left of each edge in $\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}}$ . The grading is compatible only if the resulting rectangles are non-overlapping. The condition on the shadows can be easily read off by seeing if every blue rectangle has a red rectangle above, or if every red rectangle has a blue rectangle to the left.

*Figure 2. In the top images, we depict gradings $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ on the Dyck paths $\mathcal{P}(6,4)$ and $\mathcal{P}(7,4)$ from Example 3.16, where edges with no weight shown are assigned weight $0$ . Below, we depict the corresponding rectangular tilings. The grading $\omega_{1}$ has overlapping rectangles and hence is not compatible, while the grading $\omega_{2}$ is.*

#### Remark 5.5.

The word “tight” is coined by the tight space between blue and red rectangles.

#### Example 5.6.

(1) The grading $\omega_{2}$ as in Example 3.16 (and displayed on the right of Figure 2) is shadowed. However, it is not tight because $(d_{1},d_{2})=(7,4)$ does not satisfy $pd_{2}-qd_{1}=\pm\gcd(p,q)$ for $(p,q)=(6,4)$ .

Then $\omega$ is tight as displayed in the middle of Figure 3.

We now discuss two families of tight gradings with relevance to the rank-2 cluster scattering diagrams of affine type, i.e., $\Scat(1+x^{\ell_{1}},1+y^{\ell_{2}})$ where $\ell_{1}\ell_{2}=4$ . This connection is made explicit in Example 5.21 and Example 5.22.

#### Example 5.7.

Let $P_{1}(x)=1+p_{1,2}x^{2}$ and $P_{2}(y)=1+p_{2,2}y^{2}$ . For $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , consider the path $\mathcal{P}(2k,2k+1)$ . There are $k+1$ tight gradings of weight $p_{1,2}^{k}p_{2,2}^{k}$ , that is, tight gradings $\omega$ where $\omega(h)=2$ for exactly $k$ horizontal edges $h$ , $\omega(v)=2$ for exactly $k$ vertical edges $v$ , and $\omega(e)=0$ for all other edges $e$ .

It is straightforward to describe these gradings explicitly as follows. Fix $i\in\{0,1,\dots,k\}$ . Let $S_{\mathbf{E}}=\{u_{1+i},u_{2+i},\dots,u_{k+i}\}$ and let $S_{\mathbf{N}}=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{i}\}\cup\{v_{k+2+i},v_{k+3+i},\dots,v_{2k+1}\}$ , where the sets in the union can be empty if $i=0$ or $i=k$ . Then the grading

$$ \omega(e)=\begin{cases}2&\text{ if }e\in S_{\mathbf{E}}\cup S_{\mathbf{N}}\\
0&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

is one of the desired tight gradings, and varying the choice of $i$ yields all such tight gradings.

These are the tight gradings $\omega$ such that $\omega(h)=1$ for exactly $2k$ horizontal edges $h$ , $\omega(v)=4$ for exactly $k$ vertical edges $v$ , and $\omega(e)=0$ for all other edges $e$ .

We can describe these gradings explicitly as follows. Fix $i\in\{0,1,\dots,k-1\}$ and $s\in\{0,1\}$ , with the restriction that if $i=k$ then $s=0$ . Let $S_{\mathbf{N}}=\{v_{k+1-i},v_{k+2-i},\dots,v_{2k-i}\}$ and let $S_{\mathbf{E}}=\{u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{4k-2i-1}\}\cup\{u_{4k-2i+s}\}\cup\{u_{4k-2i+2},u_{4k-2i+3},\dots,u_{4k+1}\}$ , where the sets in the union can be empty if $i=0$ . Then the grading

$$ \omega(e)=\begin{cases}2&\text{ if }e\in S_{\mathbf{E}}\cup S_{\mathbf{N}}\\
0&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

is one of the desired tight gradings, and varying the choice of $i$ yields all but one of the $2k+1$ such tight gradings. The last tight grading can be obtained by considering $S_{\mathbf{E}}=\{u_{2k+2},u_{2k+3},\dots,u_{4k+1}\}$ and $S_{\mathbf{N}}=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{k}\}$ , with the grading $\omega$ constructed as above.
